name: William Lyon Mackenzie King
summary: King pursued gradual social reform and cooperation between labour and capital. His governments expanded social security and supported wartime and international cooperation, while imposing racially discriminatory exclusion, internment and dispossession.

universal-healthcare.rationale: He repeatedly promised nationwide health insurance and called his 1948 grants initial steps toward it, but did not implement comprehensive coverage; scholars dispute his commitment.

unions-good.rationale: His later legislation protected union recognition, bargaining and remedies against unfair labour practices, after earlier resistance.

regulate-corporations.rationale: He endorses state regulation of industrial standards to prevent less scrupulous competitors undercutting humane employers (pp.352–353).

cut-welfare.rationale: After initially resisting expansion, he enacted family allowances and advocated a national minimum of social security.

worker-ownership.rationale: He welcomes worker shareholding and co-partnership, while retaining investors and professional management (pp.296–298).

traditional-family.rationale: Introducing family allowances in 1944, he explicitly described family and home as the foundations of national life.

gradual-change.rationale: He prefers gradual adjustment of existing institutions and condemns syndicalist reliance on forcible seizure (pp.402,407).

reduce-immigration.rationale: In 1947 he encouraged increased immigration and population growth, subject to economic capacity and selective admission.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: He jointly proposed a UN commission to devise international atomic controls, inspections and disarmament safeguards.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: He defended military intervention against aggression abroad in order to preserve other peoples’ independence and liberties.

open-borders.rationale: The 1947 policy retained admission controls and restrictions on large-scale Asian immigration.

expand-nuclear.rationale: He approved construction of a Canadian reactor in 1943 and jointly advocated peaceful industrial applications in 1945.

central-planning.rationale: He doubts enduring success for an omnipotent industrial state and prefers joint control alongside individual enterprise (pp.419–420).

abolish-central-banks.rationale: His government nationalized the existing Bank of Canada in 1938 rather than abolishing central banking.

political-violence-never.rationale: He explicitly defended the decision to enter war against Germany’s aggression.

means-match-ends.rationale: He contrasts coercive syndicalism with peaceful cooperation and judges institutions by the trust and partnership they foster (pp.407–409).

conscription.rationale: After earlier opposition and a domestic-service-only policy, he authorized overseas conscription in November 1944.

total-state.rationale: He rejects subordination of all institutions and human purposes to an autocratic state (pp.396–397).

workplace-democracy.rationale: He proposes worker and community representation in corporate control, with management implementing jointly determined policy (pp.368–370).

reason-over-faith.rationale: He explicitly makes spiritual faith essential to resolving industrial and international conflict (pp.84–85).

class-collaboration.rationale: His central proposal makes labour, capital, management and community partners rather than antagonists.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: His government forcibly removed and interned Japanese Canadians on a racial basis, including Canadian-born citizens, and dispossessed them.

night-watchman-state.rationale: His government must enforce humane working conditions and guarantee minimum welfare, beyond protecting property.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: His 1938 diary opposed excessive mixing of foreign bloodlines when explaining his resistance to Jewish refugee admissions.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: His government denied Japanese Canadians equal treatment on explicitly racial grounds, despite its later limited immigration and citizenship reforms.

population-transfer.rationale: His government deported thousands of Japanese Canadians, including citizens, in 1946 and continued their coastal exclusion.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: PC 1003 required conciliation before lawful strikes and prohibited strikes during an agreement’s term.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: His 1938 diary anticipated unrest from Jewish refugee admissions; his 1947 policy still aimed to preserve the population’s existing character.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: His wartime government detained Japanese Canadians without charge or trial and confiscated property.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: His 1946 legislation generally required five years’ residence before immigrants could apply for citizenship, with shorter provision for wartime veterans.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: His law recognized both territorial birth and descent; it did not replace territorial birthright with descent alone.

social-market-economy.rationale: He combines continued individual enterprise with regulation, social minimums and shared industrial control (pp.419–420).

spiritual-nature.rationale: He says industrial and political organization should serve human spiritual development as well as material needs (pp.84–85).

defensive-wars-only.rationale: His 1939 cable justified Canada’s intervention against Germany to protect other European peoples’ independence and liberties.

arms-reduction.rationale: The declaration called for eliminating atomic and other major mass-destruction weapons through an internationally safeguarded process.

collective-bargaining.rationale: His February 1944 regulations established compulsory recognition and bargaining with majority-supported unions, reversing earlier resistance.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: The citizenship law required adequate French or English, subject to an exemption after twenty years’ continuous residence.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: His family allowances extended support broadly to families with children rather than limiting assistance to the poorest.

notes: The 1918 book was downloaded and searched across industrial, political, religious and social themes. Later enacted unemployment insurance and collective bargaining supersede earlier resistance. Postwar immigration expansion and repeal of Chinese exclusion did not end Asian admission restrictions. Health-insurance advocacy was only partly implemented. Family allowances do not establish adult basic income or payment for domestic labour; reactor research does not establish unconditional technological optimism. Other modern ecological and technology positions remain unknown. No historical inferences used.
